{{Short description|none}}
[[File:Ellipse_semi-major_and_minor_axes.svg|thumb|An ellipse has two axes and two foci]]
Unlike most other elementary shapes, such as the [[circle]] and [[square]], there is no [[closed-form expression]] for the [[perimeter]] of an [[ellipse]]. Throughout history, a large number of closed-form approximations and [[expression (mathematics)|expression]]s in terms of [[integral]]s or [[series (mathematics)|series]] have been given for the perimeter of an ellipse.

== Exact value ==
=== Elliptic integral ===
{{see also|Elliptic integral#Complete elliptic integral of the second kind}}
An ellipse is defined by two axes: the major axis (the longest diameter) of length <math>2a</math> and the minor axis (the shortest diameter) of length <math>2b</math>, where the quantities <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are the lengths of the [[semi-major and semi-minor axes]] respectively. The exact perimeter <math>P</math> of an ellipse is given by the integral<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chandrupatla |first1=Tirupathi |last2=Osler |first2=Thomas |date=2010 |title=The Perimeter of an Ellipse |url=http://web.tecnico.ulisboa.pt/~mcasquilho/compute/com/,ellips/PerimeterOfEllipse.pdf |journal=The Mathematical Scientist |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=122–131}}</ref><math display="block">P=4a\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{1-e^2\sin^2\theta}\ d\theta,</math>where <math>e</math> is the [[eccentricity (mathematics)|eccentricity]] of the ellipse, defined as<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abbott |first=Paul |year=2009 |title=On the Perimeter of an Ellipse |url=https://content.wolfram.com/sites/19/2009/11/Abbott.pdf |journal=The Mathematica Journal |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=2 |doi=10.3888/tmj.11.2-4}}</ref><math display="block">e=\sqrt{1-\frac{b^2}{a^2}}.</math>If we define the function<math display="block">E(x) = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{1-x \sin^2\theta}\ d\theta,</math>known as the [[complete elliptic integral of the second kind]], the perimeter can be expressed in terms of that function simply as<math display="block">P=4aE(e^2).</math>The integral used to find the perimeter does not have a [[closed-form solution]] in terms of [[Elementary function|elementary functions]].

=== Infinite sums ===

Another solution for the perimeter, this time using the sum of an [[infinite series]], is<ref>{{Cite web |title=Perimeter of Ellipse |url=https://www.mathsisfun.com/geometry/ellipse-perimeter.html |access-date=2025-01-25 |website=www.mathsisfun.com}}</ref><math display="block">P=
2a
\pi
\left(1-\sum_{n=1}^\infty
\frac{(2n!)^2}{(2^n\cdot n!)^4} \cdot
\frac{e^{2n}}{2n-1}
\right),</math>where <math>e</math> is the eccentricity of the ellipse.

More rapid convergence may be obtained by expanding in terms of <math>h = (a-b)^2 / (a+b)^2</math>.  Found by [[James Ivory (mathematician)|James Ivory]],<ref>{{cite journal
 |last = Ivory |first = James |author-link = James Ivory (mathematician)
 |title = A new series for the rectification of the ellipsis
 |journal = Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh
 |year = 1798
 |volume = 4
 |issue = 2
 |pages = 177–190
 |url = https://books.google.com/books?id=FaUaqZZYYPAC&pg=PA177
 |doi = 10.1017/s0080456800030817
 |s2cid = 251572677
}}</ref> [[Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel|Bessel]]<ref>{{cite journal
 |ref = {{harvid|Bessel|1825}}
 |last = Bessel |first = F. W. |author-link = Friedrich Bessel
 |translator1-first=Charles F. F. |translator1-last=Karney
 |translator2-first=Rodney E. |translator2-last=Deakin
 |journal = [[Astron. Nachr.]]
 |title = The calculation of longitude and latitude from geodesic measurements
 |year = 2010 |orig-year=1825
 |volume = 331
 |number = 8
 |pages = 852–861
 |arxiv = 0908.1824
 |doi = 10.1002/asna.201011352
 |bibcode = 2010AN....331..852K
 |s2cid = 118760590
}} English translation of {{cite journal
 |first1= F. W. | last1=Bessel
 |doi=10.1002/asna.18260041601
 |year=1825
 |bibcode=1825AN......4..241B
 |title=Über die Berechnung der geographischen Längen und Breiten aus geodätischen Vermesssungen
 | journal=[[Astron. Nachr.]] |volume=4 |issue=16 |pages =241{{ndash}}254
 |arxiv=0908.1823 | s2cid=118630614 | lang=de
}}</ref> and [[Ernst Kummer|Kummer]],<ref name="Linderholm95">{{cite journal
 |title=An Overlooked Series for the Elliptic Perimeter
 |first1=Carl E. |last1=Linderholm   |first2=Arthur C. |last2=Segal
 |journal=Mathematics Magazine |volume=68 |issue=3 |pages=216–220
 |date=June 1995
 |doi=10.1080/0025570X.1995.11996318
 |quote=The authors recently found a power series for the perimeter of an ellipse whose variable is not eccentricity and which converges considerably faster than the standard series. Not finding it in the references available to us, we imagined it might be new. However, the referee informed us that we had rediscovered one of Kummer's quadratic transformations of Gauss's hypergeometric series, dating back to 1837.
}} which cites to {{cite journal
 |last=Kummer |first=Ernst Eduard |author-link=Ernst Kummer
 |title=Uber die Hypergeometrische Reihe |lang=de
 |trans-title=About the hypergeometric series
 |journal=[[Journal für die Reine und Angewandte Mathematik]]
 |volume=15 |issue=1, 2 |year=1836 |pages=39–83, 127–172
 |doi=10.1515/crll.1836.15.39
 |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_journal-fuer-die-reine-und-angewandte-mathematik_1836_15
}}</ref> there are several equivalent ways to write it. The most concise is in terms of the [[Binomial coefficient#Binomial coefficient with n = 1/2|binomial coefficient with <math>n = 1/2</math>]], but it may also be written in terms of the [[double factorial]] or [[integer]] [[binomial coefficients]]:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \frac{P}{\pi(a+b)}
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty {1/2 \choose n}^2 h^n \\
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{(2n-3)!!}{(2n)!!}\right)^2 h^n \\
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{(2n-3)!!}{2^n n!}\right)^2 h^n \\
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{(2n-1)4^n}\binom{2n}{n}\right)^2 h^n \\
    &= 1 + \frac{h}{4} + \frac{h^2}{64} + \frac{h^3}{256} + \frac{25h^4}{16384} + \frac{49h^5}{65536} + \frac{441h^6}{2^{20}} + \frac{1089h^7}{2^{22}} + \cdots.
\end{align}</math>
The coefficients are slightly smaller (by a factor of <math>2n-1</math>) than the preceding, but also <math>e^4/16 \le h \le e^4</math> is numerically much smaller than <math>e^2</math> except at <math>h = e = 0</math> and <math>h = e = 1</math>.  For eccentricities less than 0.5 {{nobr|(<math>h < 0.005</math>),}} the error is at the limits of [[double-precision floating-point]] after the <math>h^4</math> term.<ref name="Cook23">{{cite web
 |title=Comparing approximations for ellipse perimeter
 |date=28 May 2023
 |first=John D. |last=Cook
 |website=John D. Cook Consulting blog
 |url=https://www.johndcook.com/blog/2023/05/28/approximate-ellipse-perimeter/
 |access-date=2024-09-16
}}</ref>

== Approximations ==
Exact evaluation of elliptic integrals may be impractical in some cases due to their computational complexity. As a result, several approximation methods have been developed over time.

=== Ramanujan's approximations ===
Indian mathematician [[Srinivasa Ramanujan]] proposed multiple approximations.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roberts |first=Martin |date=2019-02-11 |title=A Formula for the Perimeter of an Ellipse |url=https://extremelearning.com.au/a-formula-for-the-perimeter-of-an-ellipse/ |access-date=2025-01-25 |website=Extreme Learning |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=Villarino>{{Cite arXiv |last=Villarino |first=Mark B. |date=20 June 2005 |title=Ramanujan's Perimeter of an Ellipse |eprint=math/0506384}}</ref>

==== First approximation ====
<math display="block">P\approx\pi\left(3(a+b)-\sqrt{(3a+b)(a+3b)}\right).</math>

==== Second approximation ====
<math display="block">P\approx\pi(a+b)\left(1+\frac{3h}{10+\sqrt{4-3h} }\right),</math>where <math>h=\frac{(a-b)^2}{(a+b)^2}</math>.

====Final approximation====

The final approximation in Ramanujan's notes was an improvement on his second approximation. It is regarded as one of his most mysterious equations.<math display="block">\begin{align}
  P
    &\approx \pi\left( (a+b) \left(1+\frac{3h}{10+\sqrt{4-3h} }\right)+\varepsilon \right) \\
    &\approx \pi\left( (a+b) + \frac{3(a-b)^{2}}{10(a+b)+\sqrt{a^{2}+14ab+b^{2}}}+\varepsilon\right)
\end{align}</math>where <math display="inline">\varepsilon \approx \dfrac{3ae^{20}}{2^{36}}</math> and <math>e</math> is the eccentricity of the ellipse.<ref name="Villarino" />

Ramanujan did not provide any rationale for this formula.

{{Collapse top|title=Derivation of Ramanujan's approximations}}
'''Second Approximation'''

Ramanujan's second approximation formula follows from the series representation of the perimeter of an ellipse. The expansion of the general form,

<math>1+\frac{A h}{B+\sqrt{1-C h}}=1+\frac{A}{B+1}h+\frac{A C}{2 (B+1)^2}h^2+\frac{A C^2(B+3)}{8 (B+1)^3}h^3+\cdots,</math> 

can be compared to the first three terms of the infinite series,

<math>\frac{P}{\pi(a+b)} = 1 + \frac{1}{4}h + \frac{1}{64}h^2 + \frac{1}{256}h^3  +\frac{25}{16384}h^4 + \frac{49}{65536}h^5 \cdots,</math>

to show that

<math>\frac{A}{B+1}=\frac{1}{4},  \quad \frac{A C}{2 (B+1)^2}=\frac{1}{64}, \quad \frac{A C^2(B+3)}{8 (B+1)^3}=\frac{1}{256}.</math>

Solving the system of equations, we find

<math>
A=\frac{3}{2},  \quad B=5, \quad C=\frac{3}{4}.
</math>

Substituting the values into the original equation and simplifying algebraically yields Ramanujan's second approximation formula. This formula is accurate up to the fourth coefficient of the series expansion for the perimeter of an ellipse.

'''Final Approximation'''

Mathematician Mark Villarino demonstrated that each coefficient in the series representation of Ramanujan's approximation, beyond the fourth, is less than that of the exact perimeter's series representation. He also proved that the error in Ramanujan's approximation is

<math>\varepsilon = \pi (a+b)\cdot\theta\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right)^{10}</math>

where <math display="inline">\theta</math> is a monotonically increasing function on the interval <math>0 \le \frac{a-b}{a+b} \le 1</math> and

<math>\frac{3}{2^{17}} < \theta\left( \frac{a-b}{a+b} \right) \le \frac{14}{11}\left(\frac{22}{7}-\pi\right).</math>

<ref name="Villarino" />  By taking <math display="inline">\theta</math>'s lower bound, substituting <math display="inline">\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right)^{10}</math> for the equivalent form <math display="inline">\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{1-e^2}}{1+\sqrt{1-e^2}}\right)^{10}</math>, and writing its truncated series representation <math display="inline">\left(\frac{e^2}{4}\right)^{10}</math>, one can reconstruct the error correction term Ramanujan used in his final approximation:

<math>\varepsilon \approx \pi (a+b)\cdot\left(\frac{3}{2^{17}}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{e^2}{4}\right)^{10}=\pi (a+b)\cdot\dfrac{3ae^{20}}{2^{36}}.</math>

A slightly more precise approximate form can be produced by leaving the  <math display="inline">\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right)^{10}</math> term intact:

<math>P \approx \pi(a+b)\left(1+\frac{3h}{10+\sqrt{4-3h} }+  \frac{3h^5}{2^{17}}\right)</math>

where <math>h=\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right)^2</math>.
